title: Template and target-site recognition by human LINE-1 in retrotransposition
abstract: The long interspersed element-1 (LINE-1, hereafter L1) retrotransposon has generated nearly one-third of the human genome and serves as an active source of genetic diversity and human disease<sup>1</sup>. L1 spreads through a mechanism termed target-primed reverse transcription, in which the encoded enzyme (ORF2p) nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription of its own or non-self RNAs<sup>2</sup>. Here we purified full-length L1 ORF2p and biochemically reconstituted robust target-primed reverse transcription with template RNA and target-site DNA. We report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the complete human L1 ORF2p bound to structured template RNAs and initiating cDNA synthesis. The template polyadenosine tract is recognized in a sequence-specific manner by five distinct domains. Among them, an RNA-binding domain bends the template backbone to allow engagement of an RNA hairpin stem with the L1 ORF2p C-terminal segment. Moreover, structure and biochemical reconstitutions demonstrate an unexpected target-site requirement: L1 ORF2p relies on upstream single-stranded DNA to position the adjacent duplex in the endonuclease active site for nicking of the longer DNA strand, with a single nick generating a staggered DNA break. Our research provides insights into the mechanism of ongoing transposition in the human genome and informs the engineering of retrotransposon proteins for gene therapy.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This Nature article has already attracted substantial scholarly attention, with 67 citations and standing in the top 1% most-cited papers for its field and year. The record also shows 72 documented downstream reuse events, 5 online mentions, and a small but visible public discussion footprint, indicating that the paper has influenced both research follow-on and broader scientific conversation.

Full narrative

Akanksha Thawani, Alfredo Jose Florez Ariza, Eva Nogales, and Kathleen Collins report a mechanistic study of human LINE-1 retrotransposition that has quickly become a reference point in the transposable-element literature. The article addresses how L1 ORF2p recognizes template and target DNA during target-primed reverse transcription, a problem central to understanding how L1 shapes human genome variation and disease.

The uptake pattern is strong and fairly immediate. OpenAlex records 67 citations, and the paper is ranked in the top 1% most-cited works for its field and publication year. That citation base is complemented by a reuse graph showing 72 downstream uses across articles, preprints, reviews, and other scholarly outputs, suggesting the study is being incorporated into ongoing research rather than remaining an isolated result.

The citing landscape shows the paper being taken up across a broad range of venues, with especially visible presence in preprints and in journals spanning genome editing, molecular biology, genetics, and transposable-element research. Recent citing works connect the study to topics such as L1 mutagenesis, DNA repair, neurodegeneration, and retrotransposon-based genome engineering, which is consistent with the paper’s relevance beyond a single subfield.

There is also evidence of public-facing attention, though on a smaller scale than the scholarly uptake. Crossref event data captures five online mentions, including Nature Asia and Phys.org coverage, both framing the work in accessible terms for a broader audience. Scite reports 9 supporting citation statements and 1 contradicting statement, indicating that the paper is being actively used and discussed in the literature rather than merely cited in passing.

Funding support came from the Damon Runyon Postdoctoral Fellowship, NIGMS NIH HHS awards, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and NHLBI NIH HHS, underscoring that the work sits at the intersection of basic mechanistic biology and biomedical relevance. Overall, the record points to a highly visible and rapidly integrated contribution whose influence is already extending into adjacent areas of genome engineering, DNA repair, and disease-focused transposable-element research.
